lesson.title: pop(): The Only Removal Method That Hands Something Back
lesson.summary: How .pop() removes an element, defaulting to the last one, and uniquely returns the removed value instead of returning None like the other mutating methods.
lesson.body:
append, insert, and remove all share one behavior you have now seen three times: they mutate the list in place and return None. pop breaks that pattern on purpose. It still mutates the list, removing an element from it, but it also hands that element back to you as the result of the call, which makes it the method to reach for whenever you plan to actually use the value you are taking out, rather than just discard it.

The syntax is list.pop() or list.pop(index). Called with no argument, pop removes and returns the last element of the list, using -1 as its default index behind the scenes. Called with an index, positive or negative, it removes and returns the element at that specific position instead, exactly like the indexing rules you already know. If you call pop on an empty list, or with an index that does not exist, Python raises an IndexError, the same category of error you saw with out-of-range indexing.

stack = [10, 20, 30, 40]
last = stack.pop()
print(last)
print(stack)

first = stack.pop(0)
print(first)
print(stack)

Trace this precisely. stack starts as [10, 20, 30, 40]. stack.pop() with no argument removes the last element, 40, and returns it, so last is assigned 40, while stack itself shrinks to [10, 20, 30]. The first two prints show 40, then [10, 20, 30]. Next, stack.pop(0) removes the element at index 0, which is 10, and returns it, so first is assigned 10; the remaining elements, 20 and 30, shift left to fill the gap, leaving stack as [20, 30]. The last two prints show 10, then [20, 30].

This behavior is exactly what makes lists useful as a stack, a data structure where you add and remove from the same end, last in, first out. Calling append to push a new value onto the end and pop() with no argument to remove the most recently added value is a pairing you will see constantly, including in recursive algorithms that track their own call history and in undo features that need to know the most recent action taken.

There is also a performance story worth knowing here, one that connects directly back to append and insert. pop() with no argument, removing from the end, is fast and stays fast no matter how long the list is, for the same reason append is fast: nothing else in the list has to move. pop(0), removing from the front, is slower on a long list, because every remaining element has to shift one position to the left to close the gap, the exact same shifting cost you saw discussed for insert. If you find yourself repeatedly popping from the front of a very long list, that is usually a sign a different data structure would serve the task better, though a plain list works perfectly well for the list sizes you will typically encounter in this course.

With pop in hand, you now have the full removal picture: del and remove both discard a value and give back nothing, while pop discards a value and gives it back, and choosing between them comes down to whether your program still needs that value after it leaves the list.
